extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and problem-solvers learning enumerative combinatorics
extracted.subtask_description: Methods, paradigms, and problem-solving guidance for enumerative combinatorics: counting principles (sum/product rules), bijections, recursions, inclusion–exclusion, reflection principle, coding (Prüfer), and related techniques with examples and pitfalls. Intended to teach how to set up counts, derive recurrences, and construct bijections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product Rule (Multiply choices)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a procedure is performed in sequence with independent choices at each step, multiply the number of possibilities for each choice to get the total number of outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to count sequences/words and along directed-paths: "Multiply along the paths and add up the path products." Examples: an n-set has 2^n subsets (each element in/out), there are n! permutations of an n-set, number of paths from S to G equals sum of products of edge-weights along paths (Fig.5.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum Rule (Add disjoint cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the objects to be counted naturally partition into disjoint types, count each type separately and add the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often used together with the product rule. Examples: partitioning triangles by number of polygon vertices among vertices of polygon (T = T0 + T1 + T2 + T3), counting partitions by type (e.g., partitions of 8-set into 4 blocks of various type-compositions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide and Conquer / Recursion paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: Split a problem into smaller copies of the same problem repeatedly until trivial cases are reached, then combine partial results to solve the original problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to recurrences; examples: tennis pairings Pn = (2n−1) P_{n−1} giving closed Pn = (2n)!/(2^n n!), partitions recursion for P_{n+1} using sizes of block containing new element, Stirling numbers recursion S(n+1,r)=S(n,r−1)+r S(n,r). When setting up recurrences, enumerate possibilities for how the new element participates (alone/in an existing block, chosen partner, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting by Bijection (Bijective proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can construct an explicit bijection between two sets A and B, and |B| is known, then |A| = |B|; such explicit constructions are called bijective or combinatorial proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often more enlightening than algebraic manipulation. The text emphasises constructing bijections (including p−q bijections) to translate hard counts into known counts. Examples: bijection between labeled trees and (n−2)-words (Prüfer code), bijection used in reflection principle for lattice paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting the same objects in two different ways (double counting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify a set of objects and count it in two distinct ways to derive an identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical use: count by selecting structure then labeling vs. selecting labels then structure. Examples: deriving binomial coefficient identities, sum identities like 1^k + 2^k + ... + n^k via partitions into types, computing Sn = sum_{k} binom(n,k) k^2 by counting committees with chairman and secretary in two ways to get n(n+1)2^{n−2}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate artificial ordering (divide by symmetry factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an enumeration method introduces an ordering not present in the combinatorial objects, correct for overcounting by dividing by the number of orderings (symmetry factor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: subconscious introduction of ordering; example: counting pairings by ordering players in a row counts each pairing many times—must divide by 2^n n! or otherwise account for permutations within pairs and permutations of pairs. Training and awareness eliminate this frequent trap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition-by-type / p–q application
rubrics_metrics.description: Decompose objects according to a parameter (e.g., number of polygon vertices among triangle vertices, number of blocks of a given size) so each part is easier to count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose partition that makes each subcount simple (e.g., triangles in polygon partitioned into T0..T3 with easy 1:1,1:5,1:4,1:1 assignments). Use the sum rule over these types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stirling numbers and their recurrences (second kind)
rubrics_metrics.description: S(n,k) = number of partitions of an n-set into k blocks. They satisfy S(n+1,r)=S(n,r−1)+r S(n,r) with S(n,1)=S(n,n)=1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by considering whether the new element is alone or joins an existing block (r choices). Useful for counting partitions and in closed-form formulas (appear naturally via product-sum reasoning). Beginners should compute small tables via the product-sum rule to internalize patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prüfer code (bijection between labeled trees and words)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bijective coding algorithm: repeatedly delete the leaf of smallest label, write down its neighbor; continue until two vertices remain — the resulting (n−2)-word is the Prüfer code; decoding reverses this process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to prove Cayley’s formula T_n = n^{n−2} for labeled trees. The code gives a one-to-one correspondence between labeled trees and (n−2)-words on [n]. Algorithms (coding/decoding) are given explicitly; missing numbers in code correspond to degree-1 vertices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection principle for lattice paths (André)
rubrics_metrics.description: To count paths that stay below/at a boundary, count all paths and subtract 'bad' ones by constructing a bijection (reflection) from bad paths to all paths from a reflected start point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Catalan numbers C_n count paths from (0,0) to (n,n) that never go above diagonal y=x: bad paths correspond bijectively to paths from (−1,1) to (n,n) obtained by reflecting initial segment up to first crossing. This yields C_n = (1/(n+1)) binom(2n,n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Inclusion and Exclusion (PIE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalization of the sum rule to overlapping sets: |A1 ∪ ... ∪ An| = sum |Ai| − sum_{i<j}|Ai∩Aj| + sum_{i<j<k}|Ai∩Aj∩Ak| − ... alternating signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via checking how many times an element in exactly k sets is counted gives 1. Applications: derangements (permutations with no fixed points) giving p_n ≈ n!/e, counting surjections via PIE, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph/state representation and reading recurrences
rubrics_metrics.description: Model constraints as walks on a directed graph with states representing last symbol(s) or equivalence classes; count words by counting walks of length n using the sum/product rules to read off recurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: counting n-words over {0,1,2} with neighboring difference ≤1 represented by 3-state graph yields recurrence x_{n+1} = 2 x_n + x_{n−1}. Use symmetry to reduce states and derive coupled recurrences, then eliminate to single recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear recurrence solution via characteristic equation
rubrics_metrics.description: Solve linear homogeneous recurrences with constant coefficients by assuming solutions of the form x_n = λ^n to get characteristic polynomial, find roots and express general solution as linear combination of root powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used after deriving recurrences (e.g., x_{n+1} = 2 x_n + x_{n−1}). Determine constants from initial conditions. Example yields closed form involving (1±√2)^{n+1} coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic interpretation of combinatorial sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide an identity by total count and interpret terms as probabilities of disjoint events; sum-of-probabilities equals 1 gives combinatorial identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: interpret binomial-like terms as probabilities of sequences of heads/tails to prove sum_{k≥0} binom(n+k,k) / 2^{n+k} = 1 by partitioning into events A_k, B_k (n+1 heads and k tails, or vice versa). Visualised by path endpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive bijections using small modifications (padding/extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: When direct counting is awkward, modify objects (e.g., extend a word by extra symbols or add sentinel elements) to make a bijection easier to describe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: counting binary n-words with exactly m occurrences of '01' built by padding with an extra 1 at start and 0 at end to force exactly m+1 transitions 1→0, converting problem to choosing (2m+1)-subset of n+1 gaps; gives binomial expression binom(n+1,2m+1).
